title: The best protein sources without meat

seo.title: Best protein sources without meat: amounts by serving
seo.meta_description: Eggs, dairy, soy foods, legumes, seitan, fish, nuts, and seeds can all provide protein without meat. Compare realistic serving amounts.
seo.search_intent: Find high-protein foods without meat and compare protein per realistic serving.

excerpt: You can get plenty of protein without meat. About 1 cup of Greek yogurt can provide 18–20 g, 5.3 oz firm tofu roughly 18–26 g, 1 cup cooked lentils about 18 g, two eggs about 13 g, and 5.3 oz edamame around 18 g. If fish is included, a 5 oz serving often provides more than 30 g.
content_html:
Removing meat does not mean living on foods with 2 or 3 grams of protein. Eggs, dairy, soy foods, legumes, and several other foods can contribute enough protein to anchor a meal; if fish is included, the list gets even broader.

Protein per realistic serving

FoodTypical servingProtein
High-protein Greek yogurt~7 oz / 200 g18–20 g
Firm tofu5.3 oz / 150 g18–26 g
Tempeh5.3 oz / 150 g~30 g
Cooked lentils~1 cup / 200 g~18 g
Edamame5.3 oz / 150 g~18 g
Eggs2 large~13 g
Cottage cheese~3/4 cup / 180 g~20–23 g
Seitan3.5 oz / 100 g~20–25 g
Cooked fish5 oz / 142 g~30–38 g

The useful point is that “without meat” does not have to mean “plant-only.” Vegetarian diets may include eggs and dairy, and some people avoiding meat still eat fish.

Soy and seitan are the most concentrated plant options

Tempeh, tofu, and textured soy protein can reach protein amounts similar to moderate portions of animal foods. Seitan is also concentrated, although its gluten protein is relatively low in lysine.

Legumes are less concentrated, but portions are larger

Cooked lentils and chickpeas are around 9 g protein per 100 g. A normal bowl may contain 180–250 g, bringing the meal into the 16–22 g range while also adding fiber.

Eggs and dairy simplify vegetarian protein

Two eggs provide about 13 g. A large bowl of Greek yogurt or cottage cheese can approach or exceed 20 g. Combined with legumes and grains, these foods make it easy to spread protein across the day.

Nuts and seeds are useful add-ons

One ounce of almonds provides about 6 g protein, while hemp seeds are closer to 9 g per ounce. They help raise the total, but their high calorie density means they usually work better as complements than as the only protein food.

The useful rule

For enough protein without meat, put a clear protein anchor in each main meal: eggs or dairy, tofu or tempeh, legumes, seitan, or fish if it fits your diet. Let grains, nuts, and seeds add to that base.

faq.question: What meat-free food has the most protein?
faq.answer: Tempeh and seitan are among the most concentrated common meat-free options. If fish is included, many fish provide 20–30 g protein per 100 g.

faq.question: Are legumes enough for protein?
faq.answer: They can absolutely be the main protein food in a meal. About 1 cup of cooked lentils provides roughly 18 g protein plus substantial fiber.

faq.question: Can nuts replace meat for protein?
faq.answer: They contribute protein, but a 1 oz serving usually provides only about 4–7 g and is calorie-dense. Nuts work better as a supplement than the sole replacement.
